newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-De Beers H1 sparkles, but eyes H2 cautiously.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-De Beers H1 sparkles, but eyes H2 cautiously.

text.p: De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd on Tuesday raised its attributable earnings for the six months ended June 1997 to $507 million from $482 million a year ago.

But outgoing chairman Julian Ogilvie Thompson said South Africa's diamond giant could see little improvement in the full-year if Angolan diamond production was affected. Most of Angola's production is in areas that have continued to be a bone of contention between former rebel movement UNITA and the Luanda government since a peace treaty ending nearly two decades of civil war was signed in 1994.
Thompson said a final contract with Russia to sell that country's diamonds through De Beers' London-based Central Selling Organisation (CSO) was another worry.

"That (improvement in the next half) depends very much... on the Angolan situation -- how much comes out of Angola over the rest of the year and on how much we think it is appropriate to buy," he told a news conference.
"The other important thing...is the final nature of the agreement, if we can get that finalised in terms of the presidential decree and the government resolution."
Angola has in recent weeks seemed to be lurching towards renewed fighting, with reports of troop build-ups and isolated skirmishes.
But Thompson said Angola's diamond production usually improved in the second half of the year.

"It's also often the case that production in Angola is usually high in the seond half than in the first half because it's a dry season. So in that assumption, one would expect things to begin to swing back. But we are not expecting them to straighten all the way as far back as in the first half."
Gary Ralfe, CSO's managing director, added: "If there were to be hostilities in Angola, that would reduce the flow of diamonds and that could have an effect on our business."
De Beers gave no figures of how much of Angola's diamonds accounted for its earnings.

De Beers and its international arm, De Beers Centenary AG, announced on Tuesday -- after taking into account taxation of $156 million, up from $105 million a year ago -- that its combined earnings reached $507 million. Its diamond account -- profit from trading and selling diamonds -- increased to $510 million from $447 million in the same period last year.

De Beers said combined earnings including the share of retained earnings of associates, were $775 million from the $683 million in the previous six months. The interim dividend was 27.4 U.S. cents, slightly up from 27.0.

De Beers said the interim earnings included an exceptional item of $75 million comprising the De Beers group's surplus, which arose from the disposal of a portion of its interest in mining house JCI Ltd, less a provision in respect of an anticipated loss on the disposal of its interest in Lonrho Plc.
The firm also expected 1997 diamonds sales to maintain 1996 levels in local currency terms, but sales would be down in dollar terms.

It added that the retail market was mixed with continuing strength in the U.S. being offset by weakness in Japan and in countries, particuarly in South East Asia, that were adversely affected by the strength of the dollar.

A change in its own intake of diamonds compared with the first half of 1996, when it was buying both Russian and Austrialian diamonds under contract, had resulted in a reduction of stocks and in long and medium term liabilities, De Beers said.

Thompson also announced that he would retire at the end of the year and that Nicky Oppenheimer, currently deputy chairman, had agreed to replace him. However, Thompson added that he had accepted Oppenheimer's request that he take on the position of deputy chairman while Oppenheimer steers the company into the next century.
